title: Variable tracking involves comparing the initial value and the final value.
body: A variable is like a label, and assignment is the act of changing the value that label refers to. If `x = 1` is followed by `x = x + 2`, the value of `x` changes to 3. When reading code, don’t just look at the initial value and stop there; you must check to see if there are any lines where a new value is assigned to the same variable. In particular, the output changes depending on which line the `print` statement appears on. This card is not intended for memorizing basic grammar; rather, it is a review card designed to help you read short code in the actual order of execution. When solving problems, first check what initial value the variable has, and then follow the sequence in which assignments, conditions, loops, function calls, and data structure accesses change that value. When selecting the correct answer, base your judgment not on familiar words, but on the value printed at the end, the value remaining in a list or dictionary, or the value returned by a function. Variable tracing is the practice of comparing initial and final values. If the same variable name is assigned a new value multiple times, the previous value is overwritten by the new one. When solving problems, briefly note the current value of each variable, and determine the final answer based on the value immediately before a `print` or `return` statement.
detail: Variable tracing is the practice of tracking which value a variable with the same name refers to on each line. If you only remember the initial value, it’s easy to overlook intermediate assignments. When the same variable name appears on both sides of an expression—such as `x = x + 2`—the previous value on the right side is calculated first, and that result is then stored back in `x`. The judgment is based on the final value at the time of the `print` statement.

title: "print" is used for screen output and is different from storing variables.
body: `print` is an operation that displays a value on the screen. Just because you use `print` on a value does not mean that value is automatically stored in a new variable. Conversely, even if you store a value in a variable, it may not appear on the screen unless you use `print`. When reading code, you must distinguish between the lines where values are calculated and the lines where they are actually printed to the screen. This card is not intended for memorizing basic grammar rules, but rather as a review tool for reading short code in its actual execution order. When solving problems, first check what initial values the variables have, and then follow the sequence in which assignments, conditions, loops, function calls, and data structure accesses change those values. When selecting the correct answer, base your judgment on the value printed at the end, the value remaining in a list or dictionary, or the value returned by a function—not on familiar words. `print` is an action that displays output on the screen; it is different from variable storage or function results. Executing `print(x)` does not reassign a new value to `x`. If a function only uses `print` and does not include a `return` statement, the result of the call is typically `None`. When reading code, you should distinguish between the value displayed on the screen, the value retained in the variable, and the value returned by the function.
detail: `print` is an operation that displays output on the screen; it is different from storing a value in a variable or a function’s `return` statement. Executing `print(x)` does not assign a new value to `x`, and if a function only uses `print` and does not return a value, the result of the call may be `None`. When reading code, it is important to distinguish between calculated values, stored values, and actual output values.

title: The if/else statement executes only one branch depending on the result of the condition.
body: In an if/else structure, the system first evaluates whether the conditional expression is True or False. If the condition is True, the if block is executed; if it is False, the else block is executed. Not both blocks are executed every time. You can tell which lines are inside the if block and which are inside the else block by looking at the indentation. These cards are not intended for memorizing basic grammar rules, but rather as review cards for reading short code in its actual execution order. When solving problems, first check what initial values the variables have, and then follow the sequence in which assignments, conditions, loops, function calls, and data structure accesses change those values. When selecting the correct answer, base your judgment not on familiar words, but on the value printed at the end, the value remaining in a list or dictionary, or the value returned by a function. When reading if and else statements, you must first determine whether the condition evaluates to True or False. If the condition is True, the lines inside the `if` block are executed; if False, the flow proceeds to the `else` block. Since the two paths are not executed simultaneously, assignments or outputs in the unselected branch do not affect the result.
detail: The `if` and `else` statements select only one branch of execution based on the result of a condition. If the condition is `True`, the `if` block is executed and the `else` block is skipped; if the condition is `False`, the `else` block is executed instead. The key point is that the two blocks are never executed simultaneously. The program follows the execution path while considering both the indentation scope and the current value of the conditional expression.

title: For cumulative totals, view the total change as shown in the table.
when_to_show: In problems involving calculating totals or counts using a `for` loop,
body: In a loop, if you see a line like `total = total + n`, `total` changes with each iteration. You can avoid confusion by writing down the initial value of `total`, the value of `n` for this iteration, and the new value of `total` after the calculation, in that order. Summing, counting, string concatenation, and list appending can all be understood as cumulative loop patterns. This card is not intended for memorizing basic syntax separately, but rather as a review tool for reading short code in the actual order of execution. When solving problems, first check what initial values the variables have, and then follow the order in which assignments, conditions, loops, function calls, and data structure accesses change those values. When selecting the correct answer, base your judgment not on familiar words, but on the value printed at the end, the value remaining in the list or dictionary, or the value returned by the function. Iterative accumulation problems involve observing how a variable like `total` changes with each iteration. You should first write down the initial value and then check the values added or the conditions that cause skips in each iteration. By creating a table that lists the current value and `total` separately, you can predict the final result much more reliably.
detail: Iterative accumulation is a problem that involves tracking how a variable—such as `total`—changes with each iteration. First, write down the initial value, then identify the values added or the conditions for skipping in each iteration. By listing the current iteration value, the `total` before the calculation, and the `total` after the calculation in a table, you can reliably follow the logic for summing, counting, and string concatenation.

title: In a list, the position and value are separate.
body: In a list, position and value are separate concepts. This card is a review card designed to have you read through a short problem in execution order after you’ve already learned about lists. A list contains multiple values in order, and `items[0]` refers to the first value. Here, 0 is not a value itself but a position number. `items[1]` does not refer to the number 1, but rather to the second value in the current list. Since `append` adds a new value to the end, the list length and the last value change after an `append` operation. It becomes even easier to confuse positions and values when concepts like `pop`, assignment, and slicing come into play. Therefore, when solving problems, first write down the initial state of the list, and update it at the end of each line to reflect how the list has changed. If you call `append(30)` on the list `[10, 20]`, the length becomes 3 and `items[-1]` becomes 30. After that, when `items[0] = 99` is executed, only the first value changes. If `append` is executed within a loop, the list can grow with each iteration, so you must write down both the number of iterations and the changes to the list. Distinguishing between lines that read values by index and lines that add values using `append` makes the final output easier to understand. Rather than memorizing syntax, this practice card is designed to help you identify the values printed at the end, the values remaining in the list, and the values returned by functions. By separating the index numbers from the actual values, you can reliably solve problems that involve `list`, `index`, and `append` together. When practicing, create a table with index numbers below the list, and redraw the table every time `append` or `pop` is executed. Indicate separately whether the value has changed, the position has changed, or the length has changed. Finally, check the printed value and the value remaining in the entire list separately. Doing this reduces mistakes caused by mixing up index numbers and actual values.
detail: Since a list stores positions and values separately, you must continuously update its current state. `items[0]` refers to the first value, `append` adds a value to the end, and assignment changes the value at a specific position. When solving a problem, write down the initial state of the list and, after completing each line, double-check the length, position, and last value.

title: A dictionary uses a key to find a value.
body: A dictionary stores keys and values as pairs. This card is a review card designed to have you read short code snippets in the order they are executed after you’ve already reviewed the definition of a dictionary. data['name'] is an expression that reads the value associated with the key "name," and scores['kim'] is an expression that retrieves the value associated with the key "kim." Assigning a value to the same key does not create a new dictionary; instead, it updates the value associated with that key. Therefore, when solving problems, you should first write down the initial state of the dictionary, then track on the next line whether a key is added, whether the value of an existing key is changed, and what value is ultimately printed. If you solve the problem by looking only at the first and second positions, as you would with a list, it’s easy to overlook the key names. When you see `get`, check whether it can handle a nonexistent key with a default value rather than immediately raising an error. When you encounter a loop like `for name in scores`, also check which key the loop variable actually points to. For lines like `scores[name] = scores[name] + 1`, it’s safer to break them down into two steps: reading the current key’s value and then storing it again. When selecting the correct answer, base your judgment on the value printed at the end, the key-value pairs remaining in the dictionary, and the value returned by the function, rather than just matching the syntax names. This card is intended for code comprehension rather than quick memorization. By tracking, line by line, the order in which assignments, conditions, loops, function calls, and data structure accesses change values, you can reduce mistakes in dictionary problems. When practicing, write potential keys on the left and value changes on the right, updating them line by line. In particular, if the same key appears more than once, the last assignment is likely to be the final value. Also, make a separate note of whether the code throws an error when a key is missing or uses a default value via `get`. Reading it this way makes the dictionary look less like a simple box and more like a table where values are retrieved by name.
detail: A dictionary is a data structure that uses keys to look up values. If a key is enclosed in square brackets, such as `data['name']`, the value associated with that key is retrieved. Assigning a value to the same key updates the existing value, and assigning a value to a key that doesn’t exist adds a new entry. When reading code, it’s helpful to keep track of the list of keys and their current values in a table-like format.

title: A function executes when it is called and returns a value using the `return` statement.
when_to_show: In problems that involve both `def` and function calls,
body: The `def` keyword is used to define a function, and the function body is executed when the function is called. When you call the function—as in `result = add(2, 3)`—the arguments are passed to the parameters, and the return value is stored in `result`. When solving function problems, distinguish between the definition line and the call line, and follow where the returned value goes. This card is not intended for memorizing basic grammar separately, but rather as a review card for reading short code in its actual execution order. When solving problems, first check what initial values the variables have, and then follow the order in which assignments, conditions, loops, function calls, and data structure accesses change those values. When selecting the correct answer, base your judgment not on familiar words, but on the value printed at the end, the value remaining in a list or dictionary, or the value returned by the function. A function executes when it is called, not when it is defined. The `def` line sets up the function, but the actual execution flow begins with the call line, where the function name is followed by parentheses. If there is a `return` statement, that value is returned to the calling location, so you must also check whether the result is stored in a variable.
detail: A function is executed when it is called, not when it is defined. The `def` line sets up the rules, while the actual execution flow begins with the call line, which consists of the function name followed by parentheses. You must follow the sequence in which the arguments are passed to the parameters, the code inside the function is executed, and the return value is sent back to the point of call.

title: For mixed problems, proceed one line at a time.
body: Mixed problems may seem difficult, but you can solve them by looking at them line by line. Organize the order of execution—which comes first: variable assignment, conditional statements, loops, lists, dictionaries, or function calls. Rather than trying to deeply analyze every unfamiliar term, you’ll get closer to the correct answer by first determining whether the current line reads, modifies, or outputs a value. These cards are not intended for memorizing basic grammar separately, but rather as review cards for reading short code in its actual execution order. When solving a problem, first check what initial value the variable has, and then follow the order in which assignments, conditionals, loops, function calls, and data structure accesses change that value. When selecting the correct answer, base your judgment not on familiar keywords, but on the value printed at the end, the value remaining in the list or dictionary, or the value returned by the function. Mixed problems involve multiple syntax elements at once, so trying to interpret them all at once can be confusing. First, write down the initial value of the variable, and then follow the code line by line—checking the conditional statements, loops, function calls, and changes to lists or dictionaries. Rather than choosing the answer immediately based on familiar function names, it is safer to base your judgment on the values that are actually printed at the end or the values returned by the function.
detail: Mixed problems involve multiple syntax elements appearing at once, so trying to parse them all at once can be confusing. First, write down the initial values of the variables, then follow along line by line through the conditional statements, loops, function calls, and changes to lists or dictionaries. Finally, choose the correct answer based on the values printed, the values returned, and the values remaining in the data structures.
